terms.grammar: conjunction: the indicative for a fact, the subjunctive for what is waited for or intended
terms.comment: After verbs of waiting: exspectā dum …, wait until; the subjunctive, because the end is looked for.

terms.grammar: conjunction: the indicative (future or future perfect for the future), or the subjunctive of what is aimed at
evidence: Ov. Met. 11.139: carpe viam, dōnec veniās ad flūminis ortūs
Liv. 1.39.2: movērī vetuisse puerum dōnec suā sponte experrēctus esset
terms.comment: Cato’s word in recipes: ūsque adeō, dōnec …, keep on until. Rare in Cicero, frequent before and after him (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: conjunction, with the indicative or subjunctive like dum
evidence: Cic. Fam. 4.3.3: quoad certior fierēs (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: carpe viam, dōnec veniās ad flūminis ortūs
phrases.english: take the road until you reach the river’s source

phrases.latin: movērī vetuisse puerum dōnec suā sponte experrēctus esset
phrases.english: she forbade anyone to move the boy until he woke up by himself

phrases.latin: ūsque adeō, dōnec cremor crassus erit factus
phrases.english: (stir) until the gruel has become thick

sources: Lewis & Short: dum · Lewis & Short: donec · Lewis & Short: quoad
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-ovidius, loci-livius, loci-cato), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
